references.text: Simeon in Jerusalem "waited for the consolation of Israel" – the same attitude of expectation as Joseph of Arimathea who "was waiting for the kingdom of God" ([ref:Luk 2:25|Luke 2:25]).
The prophetess Anna "was waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem," in the same way that Joseph of Arimathea was waiting for the kingdom of God ([ref:Luk 2:38|Luke 2:38]).

Mark's parallel account of Joseph of Arimathea, which also describes him as one who "was waiting for the kingdom of God" and who dared to go to Pilate to ask for Jesus' body ([ref:Mark 15:43|Mark 15:43]).
Matthew's parallel account of Joseph of Arimathea, where he is described as a rich man who had become a disciple of Jesus ([ref:Matt 27:57|Matthew 27:57]).
John's parallel account of Joseph of Arimathea, where he is described as a secret disciple of Jesus "for fear of the Jews" ([ref:Joh 19:38|John 19:38]).
The preceding verse describing Joseph as a member of the Council, a good and righteous man, which explains why he had not consented to the Council's decision ([ref:Luk 23:50|Luke 23:50]).

Jacob expresses his expectation: "Lord, I wait for your salvation" – a fundamental attitude of hope in God's intervention that is reflected in Joseph's expectation of the kingdom of God ([ref:1 Mos 49:18|Gen 49:18]).
The broader context in Mark regarding Joseph's bold action: he went to Pilate and asked for Jesus' body, even though he was a member of the Council ([ref:Mark 15:42-45|Mark 15:42-45]).

Jesus' parable about the guest who will "eat bread in the kingdom of God" shows the expectation of the kingdom of God among devout Jews, the same expectation that Joseph of Arimathea had ([ref:Luk 14:15|Luke 14:15]).
